## Policy question

A North Carolina maternal-health planning team has been using **12 prenatal visits per pregnancy** as an administrative workload benchmark.

For this exercise, 12 is a planning assumption, not a medical recommendation.

> **Is the observed average number of prenatal visits different enough from 12 that we should reconsider the planning assumption?**

## Setup

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

load(url("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GarciaRios/govt_3990/gh-pages/Labs/lab5/nc.RData"))

nc_visits <- nc |>
  filter(!is.na(visits))
```

## Exercise 1: Start with the data

```{r}
visit_stats <- nc_visits |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    x_bar = mean(visits),
    s = sd(visits),
    median = median(visits),
    min = min(visits),
    max = max(visits)
  )

visit_stats
```

```{r}
ggplot(nc_visits, aes(x = visits)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Prenatal visits",
    y = "Number of births",
    title = "Prenatal visits in the North Carolina sample"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Exercise 4: Standard error and test statistic

```{r}
n <- nrow(nc_visits)
x_bar <- mean(nc_visits$visits)
s <- sd(nc_visits$visits)

se <- s / sqrt(n)

mu_0 <- 12
t_obs <- (x_bar - mu_0) / se
df <- n - 1

c(
  n = n,
  x_bar = x_bar,
  s = s,
  se = se,
  t = t_obs,
  df = df
)
```

## Exercise 5: Calculate and interpret the p-value

```{r}
p_value <- 2 * pt(
  -abs(t_obs),
  df = df
)

p_value
```

## Exercise 7: Let R check our work

```{r}
visit_test <- t.test(
  nc_visits$visits,
  mu = 12,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  conf.level = 0.95
)

visit_test
```

21. Find the test statistic and p-value in the output. Do they match your calculations?

> 

22. Find the 95% confidence interval. Does 12 fall inside or outside it?

>

## Exercise 8: Change to a one-sided question

Suppose the agency instead asks whether the population mean is **greater than 12**.

```{r}
t.test(
  nc_visits$visits,
  mu = 12,
  alternative = "greater"
)
```
